chief_complaint: Elevated blood pressure with obesity, prediabetes, and chronic musculoskeletal pain
history_of_present_illness: The patient is a 58-year-old male with a long-standing history of obesity since 2001. He developed hand osteoarthritis in 2012 and chronic low back pain in 2014, which together with generalized chronic pain have been managed with over‑the‑counter naproxen. In 2017 he was diagnosed with anemia and prediabetes (A1c 6.0%). Blood pressure measured most recently at 130/90 mmHg meets criteria for stage 2 hypertension, yet no antihypertensive therapy has been prescribed. In September 2021 he transitioned to part‑time employment and reports new stress. No emergency or inpatient visits have occurred; most encounters are wellness visits.

active_problems.name: Localized primary osteoarthritis of the hand

past_medical_history: Resolved conditions include multiple medication review reminders (2020‑2021), prior full‑time employment, past social isolation (resolved 2021), viral sinusitis (2019), gingival disease and gingivitis (2018), and earlier part‑time employment (2018).
social_determinants: Lives in Cambridge, MA; currently employed part‑time; reports recent stress related to employment change; has higher education; no documented smoking, alcohol, or housing instability.
risk_factor_summary: Blood pressure 130/90 mmHg (stage 2 hypertension); BMI not recorded but obesity documented; A1c 6.0% (prediabetic); Charlson comorbidity index 1 (anemia); clinical complexity moderate. Organ systems at elevated risk: cardiovascular (hypertension, obesity, prediabetes), renal (NSAID use + hypertension, unknown eGFR), metabolic (prediabetes, likely dyslipidemia), hematologic (anemia), musculoskeletal (chronic pain, osteoarthritis), psychosocial (stress, part‑time employment).

clinical_impression: The patient presents with moderate clinical complexity driven by untreated stage 2 hypertension, obesity, and prediabetes—components of metabolic syndrome—combined with chronic musculoskeletal pain and anemia of unclear etiology. NSAID therapy for osteoarthritis adds renal and gastrointestinal risk in the setting of hypertension. Social stressors and part‑time employment may further impact disease management and adherence.
